item.title: Propertymark urges benefits increase for poorest private tenants
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Propertymark has urged the government to increase housing benefits for private renters on the lowest incomes, warning that current support levels fail to match soaring rental costs across the UK. The professional body has written to Baroness Sherlock, Minister of State at the Department for Work and Pensions, calling for reforms to the Local Housing Allowance (LHA) system alongside greater transparency around emergency housing funds.

Gap Between Benefits and Market Rents Widens

The trade association acknowledges that temporary crisis payments through local authorities' Crisis and Resilience Fund provide vital short-term relief. However, it argues these one-off measures cannot compensate for systemic underfunding of ongoing housing support. With LHA rates frozen since 2020 whilst private rents have risen sharply, research suggests just 2.7% of rental properties now fall within benefit caps - down from 12% in 2021.

Propertymark proposes three key reforms:

  • Restoring LHA rates to cover at least the bottom 30% of local market rents
  • Implementing annual updates to maintain parity with rental inflation
  • Eventually raising support to the 50th percentile when fiscal conditions allow

Transparency Needed on Emergency Support

The organisation has also called for detailed reporting on Crisis Fund allocations, including:

  • Application volumes and approval rates
  • Proportion of repeat claims
  • Average payment amounts towards rent shortfalls

This data would reveal how frequently households rely on emergency payments to bridge the growing gap between their benefits and actual rents. With private tenancies often the only option for low-income households amid social housing shortages, sustained underfunding of housing support risks increasing rent arrears, evictions and homelessness.

Whilst recognising LHA isn't designed to cover all rents in all areas, Propertymark warns that the current disconnect between benefit levels and market realities places unsustainable pressure on both vulnerable tenants and local authority budgets. The body's intervention highlights the need for long-term solutions alongside temporary crisis measures in the private rental sector.

item.title: Home ownership set to become Britain’s biggest financial divide
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Home ownership could become the most significant financial divide in Britain by 2050, according to a new report from the Building Societies Association (BSA). The study, titled "Finance for a Fairer Future", suggests that property ownership may increasingly depend on inherited wealth rather than personal savings or earnings, potentially widening the gap between homeowners and renters over the next three decades.

The growing housing wealth gap

The BSA's analysis paints a concerning picture of Britain's future financial landscape. Without intervention, the report warns that housing market inequality could deepen significantly, creating stark generational divides. Many parents and grandparents already fear their children may never achieve the same property ownership milestones they enjoyed.

While housing affordability remains an immediate challenge, the report identifies this as part of a broader financial shift. Future generations may face multiple pressures including unpredictable incomes, higher debt levels, reduced savings and less secure retirement provisions. These factors could leave households shouldering greater financial risks than ever before.

Interestingly, the report notes that even home ownership may no longer guarantee financial stability. Property owners could face mounting costs for climate-related home improvements, age-adaptation works, later-life care expenses and assisting younger family members onto the housing ladder. Housing wealth may increasingly become the primary asset families use to support multiple generations.

Broader financial resilience concerns

The BSA's findings extend beyond housing to wider financial vulnerabilities. Technological changes reshaping the job market may lead to more volatile incomes for many workers. Combined with rising student debt, limited savings and the shift from final salary pensions, individuals may need to manage greater financial complexity throughout their lives.

The report highlights how artificial intelligence could transform financial services, but warns that increasing automation might exclude some consumers. As financial lives grow more complex, the BSA suggests the industry may need to develop new products and services that better reflect modern realities, including:

  • Support for those with irregular incomes
  • Improved financial wellbeing guidance
  • More flexible approaches to lending and saving

With an ageing population and pressure on public finances, the report suggests individuals may need to take greater responsibility for funding their later-life needs. This potential shift could make early financial planning even more crucial for future generations.

While the report outlines significant challenges, it also serves as a timely reminder of the importance of long-term financial planning. Homeowners and prospective buyers might consider how these trends could affect their own financial futures and those of their families.

item.title: Are homes ready for Burnham’s home care plans?
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

As the UK's population ages, more families are considering how to help elderly relatives remain in their homes comfortably and safely. With Andy Burnham’s recent focus on home-based social care, questions arise about whether properties are suitably adapted for older occupants. Research shows growing interest in elderly care solutions, with online searches for 'elderly home care' rising sharply in recent months.

The challenge of ageing in place

For many older people, staying in their own home represents independence and familiarity. However, properties designed for younger, mobile individuals may present increasing challenges as mobility declines. Everyday activities like climbing stairs or navigating narrow doorways can become significant obstacles. Housing experts note that simple modifications could make homes more accessible, yet many properties lack basic adaptations.

Neil McKenzie, a home safety specialist, emphasises that care planning should include assessing physical living spaces: "While discussions often focus on care provision, we must also consider whether homes can practically support ageing residents. Recognising early signs of difficulty – such as avoiding stairs or struggling with bathroom access – allows families to implement safety improvements before accidents occur."

Practical home adaptations

Experts suggest several cost-effective modifications that could help older residents maintain independence:

  • Installing grab rails in bathrooms and hallways
  • Replacing traditional door handles with lever-style versions
  • Improving lighting in hallways and staircases
  • Removing trip hazards like loose rugs or clutter
  • Considering stairlifts for multi-level properties

The Office for National Statistics projects the over-65 population could grow by nearly 10 million within 50 years, making home accessibility an increasingly important consideration. While major renovations might be costly, smaller changes could significantly enhance safety and quality of life for elderly residents.

As the national conversation about social care evolves, homeowners with ageing relatives might wish to assess their property's suitability for future needs. Early planning could help avoid rushed decisions when mobility challenges arise, potentially allowing loved ones to remain in familiar surroundings for longer.

item.title: Four million pets to move into rental property this year
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Nearly four million renters in England have brought a pet into their home – or plan to do so – during 2026, following landmark changes under the Renters' Rights Act. Research from Simply Business reveals 44% of tenants have either welcomed a furry companion this year or intend to, with 12% acting within weeks of the reforms coming into force on 1 May.

Tenant Rights and Landlord Considerations

The updated legislation gives tenants the right to request permission to keep pets, with landlords required to consider each application individually. Whilst landlords cannot unreasonably refuse these requests, they may implement safeguards against potential pet-related damage. Younger renters appear particularly enthusiastic about the changes, with 18% of 25-34 year-olds acquiring pets shortly after the reforms took effect, and a further 37% planning to do so this year. In contrast, 64% of renters aged over 55 have no current plans to introduce a pet to their household.

Protecting Rental Properties

Most pet-owning tenants (93%) are taking proactive steps to safeguard their rented accommodation. Popular precautions include regular deep cleaning (adopted by over half of respondents), using pet gates to restrict access to certain rooms (39%), and fitting protective, machine-washable covers on furniture (38%). Dogs remain the preferred choice for 58% of new pet owners, while 43% have opted for feline companions.

Alex Woolf of Simply Business noted: "Renters are clearly delighted to welcome pets into their homes. Whilst it's encouraging to see tenants taking responsibility, accidental damage can still occur. With pet deposits no longer permitted under recent reforms, landlords may wish to explore alternative protection measures."

In response to these changes, Simply Business has introduced Pet Property Damage insurance for landlords. This new product offers up to £5,000 of cover for accidental damage to fixtures and fittings caused by pets, with no excess payable. Julie Fisher, UK CEO at Simply Business, commented: "As the Renters' Rights Bill transforms the rental landscape, we're committed to helping landlords adapt confidently to these regulatory changes while supporting tenants' growing desire for pet ownership."

For both landlords and tenants, these developments represent a significant shift in the rental market, balancing animal companionship with property protection in England's private rented sector.

item.title: Largest August price drop since 2018, says Rightmove
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New data from Rightmove reveals the largest August house price drop since 2018, with average asking prices falling by 2.0% (£7,360) this month to £364,999. Whilst seasonal dips are typical during the summer months, this year's decline exceeds the ten-year average of -1.3%, signalling a more competitive market for sellers.

Market conditions favour buyers

The property portal notes that available housing stock has reached a 12-year high for this time of year, coinciding with the traditionally slower summer period. This combination of increased supply and reduced buyer activity has led many sellers to adjust their price expectations downwards. The average asking price now sits 1.0% below August 2022 levels - the most significant annual decline since December last year.

Rightmove's property expert Colleen Babcock observes: "The current market reality means many sellers are adopting more competitive pricing strategies from the outset. With buyers facing the widest property selection in over a decade, pricing appropriately has become crucial."

Regional variations in price movements

The national figures conceal notable regional disparities in property price performance. Northern England has seen average asking prices rise by 1.5% annually, while southern regions recorded a 1.8% decrease. London continues to experience the most pronounced downward pressure, with prices falling 3.1% year-on-year.

The capital presents particular challenges, with available properties reaching a 16-year high - significantly above the national trend. Affordability remains a key concern, with London homes costing approximately 17 times the average annual wage despite recent wage growth outpacing property price increases.

Marc von Grundherr of Benham and Reeves comments: "London's market faces unique pressures this year, with affordability constraints playing a central role in current conditions."

For those considering a move, the current market offers both opportunities and challenges. The increased choice and more competitive pricing may benefit buyers, whilst sellers might need to carefully consider their pricing strategy to attract attention in a busier marketplace.

item.title: UK property market takes an unexpected 11% summer knock
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property market has seen an unexpected 11% weekly drop in sales agreed during what is typically a quieter summer period. Whilst seasonal slowdowns are common, the scale of this decline has raised eyebrows amongst industry observers, particularly following two unusually strong weeks that defied normal summer trends.

Market fluctuations or emerging trend?

Estate agents and prospective buyers may wish to monitor whether this represents a temporary blip or the beginning of a more significant shift. The figures from week ending 9th August 2026 show 21,800 homes sold subject to contract - down from 24,700 the previous week but still 10.6% higher than the same period in 2023. With net residential sales for the year to date standing at 591,000, the market remains 4.2% above pre-pandemic levels.

New property listings also saw a modest dip, with 31,500 homes coming to market compared to 32,800 the previous week. Year-to-date listings remain broadly in line with recent years, sitting just 0.3% below 2025 levels but 10.7% above the 2017-19 average.

Regional variations and market health indicators

Beyond the headline figures, exchanges and withdrawals provide further insight into market dynamics. July 2026 saw 65,500 exchanges (a figure likely to rise as late reports come in) against 63,400 withdrawals. This suggests just over half of properties leaving agents' books successfully completed, highlighting the importance of monitoring transaction success rates alongside initial sales agreements.

For homeowners considering entering the market, these mixed signals could indicate a period of potential opportunity. Whilst buyer demand appears to have softened slightly in the short term, the market remains fundamentally stronger than pre-pandemic levels. Those thinking of selling might wish to consider that pricing realistically from the outset could help avoid later reductions.

As always with property market movements, one week's data doesn't establish a definitive trend. However, borrowers and sellers may find it valuable to keep a close eye on whether this summer's fluctuations develop into a more sustained pattern in the coming months.

item.title: Landlords paying in cash are negotiating large discounts
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Buy-to-let investors are securing substantial property discounts by leveraging their cash reserves and chain-free status, according to recent market analysis. With the housing market showing signs of cooling, landlords accounted for 14.1% of all UK property purchases in July 2026 – a notable increase from the 12.4% year-to-date average. The data reveals investors are becoming increasingly bold with their offers, capitalising on softening demand to negotiate better deals.

Investors driving harder bargains

The latest figures show landlords paid an average of just 88.7% of asking prices in July 2026, with over half (56%) of investor offers coming in at least 10% below the initial listing price. This represents the highest proportion of deep discounts since April 2020. Cash buyers proved particularly aggressive, with 63% of cash-backed landlord offers in England and Wales starting at 10% or more under the asking price.

By comparison, traditional buyers showed more restraint. Only 25% of first-time buyer offers and 27% of home mover bids ventured into double-digit discount territory. The growing acceptance of lower offers suggests sellers are becoming more realistic about market conditions, with 27% of substantial investor discounts being accepted in July 2026 versus just 18% a year earlier.

Regional variations in discount hunting

Market dynamics vary significantly across regions, with Southern England (excluding London) seeing the most aggressive discounting. The South East led the trend, where 70% of investor offers came in at least 10% below asking price, followed by the South West at 60%. However, sellers in these regions proved more resistant – only 54% of deep-discount offers succeeded in the South East, falling to 44% in the South West.

Flats appear particularly vulnerable to price reductions, with leasehold sellers accepting 41% of offers at 10% or more below asking price. This reflects ongoing challenges in the apartment market, where demand remains subdued. Properties that attracted investor interest typically spent just 45 days on the market before accepting offers within 10% of the asking price, suggesting motivated sellers are prioritising certainty over maximum price.

For homeowners considering selling to investors, these figures highlight the importance of realistic pricing strategies in the current climate. Meanwhile, landlords with available capital may find increasing opportunities to acquire properties at favourable prices, particularly in the leasehold sector and southern regions outside London.

item.title: New collaboration between Land Registry and Ordnance Survey
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Two of Britain’s most established property data organisations have joined forces in a landmark partnership designed to modernise the housing market. HM Land Registry (HMLR) and Ordnance Survey (OS) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding that could streamline property transactions and improve data accessibility across England and Wales.

A Digital Leap for Property Transactions

The collaboration marks a significant step in HMLR’s digital transformation strategy, building upon its 2025+ vision to make property services faster and more efficient. For over 160 years, HMLR has maintained official records of land ownership, while OS has provided critical geospatial data used in land registration. The new partnership aims to bridge these datasets, potentially reducing administrative hurdles for homeowners, businesses and developers.

Ordnance Survey’s detailed mapping plays a crucial role in property transactions, with over 4,500 case workers daily using its data to update land registers and visualise property boundaries. The integration of these systems could lead to quicker processing times and fewer discrepancies in title plans – factors that currently contribute to delays in property purchases.

Benefits for the Housing Market

The enhanced data sharing between these government bodies may deliver several advantages:

  • Improved accuracy in property records and boundary definitions
  • Faster processing of land registration applications
  • Better visibility of new housing developments for prospective buyers
  • Stronger foundations for government housing policies

Tina Kennedy, OS Chief Customer Officer, highlighted the economic importance of the initiative: “A more efficient property market supports everything from home moves to infrastructure development. Our collaboration with HMLR represents a valuable opportunity to enhance services for homeowners and property professionals alike.”

The three-year partnership forms part of wider efforts to digitise Britain’s property sector. With both organisations having undergone significant technological upgrades in recent years, the stage is set for more connected, data-driven property services that could benefit all market participants.

As the property market continues to evolve, such collaborations may become increasingly important in maintaining an efficient, transparent system that supports both individual homeowners and the wider economy.

item.title: Households earning £100m a year exporting solar power
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

UK households using solar panels have collectively earned nearly £100 million in the past year by exporting surplus electricity back to the grid through Octopus Energy. With over 400,000 homes participating in the supplier's export tariff scheme, the average household received £244 for contributing clean energy. The recent summer heatwave saw a notable surge in interest for solar technology. Between May and July, Octopus recorded 74,000 enquiries about solar panel installations - a 34% increase compared to the same period in 2022. On 26th June, the hottest day recorded this year, solar-related enquiries peaked at 50% above the monthly average.

Perhaps more striking is the dramatic 630% year-on-year growth in enquiries about standalone battery storage systems during the three summer months. Home batteries allow households to store cheap off-peak electricity for later use or sell surplus solar power back to the grid when wholesale prices are highest, potentially improving the financial returns from renewable energy investments.

These developments suggest that the case for domestic renewable energy is becoming increasingly compelling. Homeowners considering solar installations now have multiple factors to weigh - potential earnings from excess power exports, reduced household emissions, and greater energy independence alongside traditional considerations like installation costs and property suitability.

As energy prices remain volatile and environmental concerns grow, renewable home energy solutions appear to be moving from niche appeal to mainstream consideration. With financial incentives aligning with ecological benefits, solar panels and battery storage may become a more common sight across British rooftops in coming years.

item.title: How Should Landlords Respond to AI-Generated Tenant Complaints?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords may increasingly find themselves facing unexpected tenant complaints drafted with the help of artificial intelligence (AI). These letters can be lengthy, complex, and filled with legal references, leaving landlords unsure how to respond. Whilst AI-generated complaints might seem intimidating, understanding how to handle them effectively could help landlords navigate these situations with confidence.

Recognising AI-Generated Complaints

One of the first signs that a complaint may have been drafted using AI is a sudden change in the tenant’s communication style. AI-generated letters often include detailed legal arguments, cite obscure legislation, and adopt a formal tone that differs from the tenant’s usual correspondence. Whilst these letters may appear authoritative, it’s worth noting that AI tools can sometimes misinterpret or misapply the law.

Landlords should take AI-generated complaints seriously, as they usually stem from genuine tenant concerns. However, it could be beneficial to approach the letter with caution, particularly when it comes to the accuracy of the legal claims. Verifying the legitimacy of the cited laws and understanding the core issue being raised might help landlords formulate an appropriate response.

Analysing the Complaint

When faced with a complex complaint, landlords might consider breaking it down into manageable sections. Using AI tools to analyse the letter could help identify the key issues, allegations, and requested actions. For example, landlords could ask the AI to summarise the complaint into categories such as the problem raised, evidence provided, and deadlines requested. This approach might make it easier to understand the tenant’s concerns without becoming overwhelmed by legal jargon.

It’s important to separate the tenant’s core issue from the legal arguments they present. For instance, if the complaint cites damp issues under Awaab’s Law or alleges a missing gas safety certificate, landlords could focus on resolving the underlying problem rather than debating the legal details. Addressing the practical concerns promptly might help de-escalate the situation.

Seeking Reliable Advice

Whilst AI tools can provide useful insights, landlords should avoid relying solely on them for legal advice. AI-generated responses can be prone to errors, just as the tenant’s letter might contain inaccuracies. Instead, landlords might consider using AI to organise and clarify the complaint before seeking professional guidance if needed.

For those unsure about the next steps, consulting organisations such as the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) or local council housing teams could provide reliable support. These resources might offer clarity on legal obligations and help landlords respond appropriately to tenant complaints.

AI-generated tenant complaints may initially appear daunting, but landlords who approach them methodically could find them easier to manage. By focusing on the core issue, verifying legal claims, and seeking reliable advice, landlords might ensure a fair and effective resolution for both parties.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #449
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property market has seen significant developments this week, with issues ranging from rising tenancy fraud to increased Right to Buy sales and proposals for stricter penalties for landlords. These changes could have far-reaching implications for homeowners, tenants, and property investors alike.

AI-Driven Tenancy Fraud on the Rise

Recent research by Goodlord has highlighted a worrying trend in the rental market: fraudulent tenancy applications are becoming increasingly sophisticated, costing landlords and letting agents an average of £9,600 per tenancy. Scammers are using artificial intelligence to create convincing fake documents, such as bank statements, employment references, and IDs, making it harder for landlords to verify tenant information. Over the past year, tenancy fraud has surged by 40%, with the overall cost to the industry now estimated at £4.1 billion annually.

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has urged landlords to remain vigilant, describing the report as a "wake-up call" for the sector. With fraudsters becoming more adept at exploiting technology, property owners might consider implementing stricter verification processes to mitigate risks.

Right to Buy Sales Surge

Government data has revealed a significant increase in Right to Buy sales, with 14,275 council homes sold in England during 2025-26. This marks a 90% rise compared to the previous year, potentially driven by tenants rushing to take advantage of the scheme before new rules come into effect. These changes will extend the minimum eligibility period and reduce the discounts available to buyers.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, has raised concerns about the impact of these sales on the wider housing market. With social housing stock dwindling, the need for replacement homes has become increasingly urgent. The Resolution Foundation reports that 1.3 million households are currently on local authority waiting lists, the highest number since 2014. Many low-income families are left with no choice but to rent more expensive private accommodation, exacerbating the housing crisis.

Proposed Fines for Landlords

Local authorities are also considering stricter enforcement measures for landlords. For instance, Bath & North East Somerset Council has proposed heavy fines for property owners who fail to meet regulatory standards. However, councils must adhere to their enforcement policies and cannot impose penalties arbitrarily. These measures aim to improve housing conditions and protect tenants, but they could also place additional financial burdens on landlords.

As the property market continues to evolve, homeowners, tenants, and landlords alike may need to stay informed about these developments. From tackling tenancy fraud to addressing housing shortages, the challenges facing the sector are complex and multifaceted. Keeping abreast of these changes could help individuals make informed decisions in an increasingly unpredictable market.

item.title: The Property Upgrades Tenants Notice Most When Viewing a Rental Home
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With the UK rental market more competitive than ever, landlords seeking to attract quality tenants might consider targeted property upgrades that maximise appeal during viewings. Research suggests certain improvements significantly influence tenant decisions, potentially reducing void periods and supporting stronger rental yields. So which features do renters prioritise?

First Impressions: Curb Appeal & Cleanliness

Tenants often form opinions within seconds of arriving, making exterior presentation crucial. Simple upgrades like repainting the front door, ensuring clear pathways, and maintaining tidy landscaping can create an instant positive impression. Inside, cleanliness reigns supreme – professional deep cleaning, fresh grout in bathrooms, and odour-neutralising treatments signal a well-maintained property.

Landlords may wish to focus on:

  • Neutral, freshly painted walls (magnolia remains a safe choice)
  • Sparkling kitchen appliances and spotless worktops
  • Bathroom fixtures free from limescale or mildew

Practical Upgrades That Add Value

Beyond aesthetics, renters frequently prioritise functional improvements that enhance daily living. Energy efficiency features like double glazing and modern boilers increasingly influence tenant decisions amidst rising utility costs. Storage solutions also rank highly – built-in wardrobes or clever under-stair cupboards can make compact spaces feel more liveable.

Other worthwhile considerations include:

  • USB charging points near beds and sofas
  • Ample, well-placed lighting (particularly in darker rooms)
  • Quality flooring that withstands wear and tear

Whilst major renovations may not always be cost-effective, small touches like replacing dated light fittings or installing a water-efficient showerhead could make a property stand out from comparable rentals.

The Kitchen: A Key Deciding Factor

Many letting agents report that kitchens disproportionately influence tenant choices. Rather than full replacements, landlords might consider cost-effective refreshes like replacing cracked tiles, updating cabinet handles, or regrouting work surfaces. Ensuring appliances are in good working order is essential – tenants often test taps, ovens and extractor fans during viewings.

The rental market shows no signs of slowing, meaning strategic investments in property presentation could prove valuable for landlords aiming to secure dependable, long-term tenants. By focusing on upgrades that genuinely matter to renters, property owners may achieve better returns without undertaking prohibitively expensive renovations.

item.title: Unfreezing housing benefits will not drive up rents
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research challenges the assumption that increasing housing benefit payments would automatically push up private rental prices across the UK. As the government considers whether to extend the current freeze on Local Housing Allowance (LHA) rates beyond April 2025, analysis from the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) suggests no direct correlation between benefit levels and rent inflation.

The impact of frozen housing benefits

LHA rates, which determine how much housing benefit private renters can claim, were originally designed to cover the lowest 50% of local market rents when introduced in 2008. Following cuts in 2011, this was reduced to the bottom 30% of rents. The current freeze means fewer than 2% of private rentals remain affordable for benefit recipients, according to homelessness charity Crisis.

Historical data reveals an interesting pattern: between 2008-2016 when LHA rates rose annually with rents, average weekly rents increased by 2.5% per year. However, during the 2016-2024 period when rates were mostly frozen, rents actually rose faster at 3.4% annually. This suggests other market factors may have greater influence on rental prices than benefit levels.

Potential benefits of adjusting LHA rates

Experts highlight several advantages to realigning housing support with current market rents. The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimates maintaining LHA at the 30th percentile would cost £1.5bn annually - significantly less than the £2.8bn councils spent on temporary accommodation last year.

Research from the Resolution Foundation indicates that restoring LHA rates could have substantial social benefits:

  • Covering the lowest 30% of rents might lift 75,000 children and 125,000 adults out of poverty
  • Returning to the original 50th percentile could help 130,000 children and 215,000 adults escape poverty

With approximately one quarter of private renters receiving housing support, the current freeze has created significant affordability challenges across many regions. The IFS has cautioned that fiscal constraints shouldn't justify a system that creates uncertainty for renters and regional inequalities.

As the debate continues, housing advocates argue that evidence increasingly shows maintaining frozen benefit rates may be doing little to control rents while exacerbating housing insecurity for vulnerable tenants. The government faces difficult choices balancing welfare spending with ensuring adequate housing support.

item.title: Air-conditioning searches double as 61% consider installation
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

As Britain experiences increasingly warm summers, new data suggests homeowners are prioritising cooling features when searching for properties. Rightmove reports a 104% surge in searches for homes with air conditioning compared to last summer, while over 60% of households now contemplate installing cooling systems.

Heatwaves reshaping property priorities

Recent Rightmove research surveying 1,062 adults reveals only 11% find their homes remain comfortable during heatwaves, with 45% struggling to maintain cool temperatures indoors. This shift in climate awareness appears to be influencing housing decisions, with 87% of respondents considering a property's summer cooling capabilities important when moving home.

Property expert Colleen Babcock notes: "Whilst location and affordability remain fundamental factors, we're seeing buyers pay closer attention to how homes perform in warmer weather. The market is responding to this growing demand, with more prospective buyers actively searching for properties featuring built-in cooling solutions."

Homeowners adapt to rising temperatures

Many households are already implementing practical measures to combat summer heat:

  • 56% have installed improved window coverings like blackout blinds or reflective film
  • 48% use fans as their primary cooling method
  • 38% have upgraded insulation to regulate indoor temperatures
  • 29% have added garden shading through trees or structures

Estate agents report growing interest in energy-efficient cooling solutions. Mark Wiggin of Mark Wiggin Estate Agents observes: "We're seeing heightened demand for properties with air source heat pumps, solar panels and integrated air conditioning systems. International buyers often expect these features as standard, and UK buyers are increasingly following suit."

Whilst only 12% of homeowners currently have air conditioning installed, 61% would consider adding it. Other popular considerations include external shading (58%) and improved ventilation systems (52%). These trends suggest that Britain's changing climate may permanently alter what buyers look for in residential properties.

As summer temperatures continue to rise, both homebuyers and existing homeowners appear to be re-evaluating their priorities. From search behaviour to renovation plans, staying cool has become a significant factor in Britain's housing market.

item.title: Scotland’s housing emergency decades in the making
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Scotland’s housing crisis has been decades in the making, according to a recent analysis by Scottish property firm DJ Alexander Ltd. The lettings and estate agency highlighted that a significant decline in social housing, combined with a growing population over the past 20 years, has culminated in the current emergency. Between 2007 and 2024, Scotland’s population increased by 402,700, while the number of occupied dwellings rose by just 286,142. This disparity has placed immense pressure on the housing market, with social housing availability shrinking by 20,267 properties during the same period.

The Shift in Housing Dynamics

Over the last two decades, there has been a notable shift in household demographics in Scotland. Smaller households, consisting of one or two people, have become increasingly common, while the prevalence of larger families has diminished. This change has necessitated a greater volume of homes to accommodate the population, yet the rate of property construction has failed to keep pace with demand. David Alexander, CEO of DJ Alexander Scotland, emphasised that the housing emergency is not a sudden development but a consequence of long-term trends. He noted, "Far too little social housing has been built, and the population continues to grow, with more people living alone or as couples. This has created a significant shortfall in housing supply."

The Role of the Private Rented Sector

While social housing has declined, the private rented sector (PRS) has played a crucial role in meeting housing demand. Over the past 20 years, the number of homes in the PRS has increased by 43.4%, now totalling 107,242 more properties than in 2007. This growth has helped to mitigate the lack of available social housing, providing much-needed accommodation for many. Alexander pointed out, "Without landlords and property investors, the housing shortage would have been far more severe. The private rented sector has filled a gap that the social sector has been unable to address."

Despite the rise in PRS properties, challenges remain. Homeownership has seen a slight decline in percentage terms, falling from 62% in 2007 to 60% in 2024. However, the actual number of homeowners has reached a record high of 1,645,318, reflecting an increase of nearly 100,000 over the past five years. This highlights the complex dynamics of Scotland’s housing market, where multiple sectors are struggling to meet the diverse needs of the population.

As Scotland’s housing crisis continues to unfold, it underscores the urgent need for a comprehensive strategy to address the shortfall in social housing and ensure that supply meets demand. With population growth showing no signs of slowing, the issue remains a pressing concern for policymakers and stakeholders alike.

item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent data reveals that landlords in England and Wales lodged 28,610 possession claims between April 2025 and March 2026, highlighting the ongoing complexities within the rental market. Despite high tenant demand, soaring rents, and fierce competition for properties, court proceedings remain a significant aspect of landlord-tenant relationships. These claims often stem from issues such as rent arrears, breaches of tenancy agreements, or antisocial behaviour, though they do not always result in evictions or possession orders.

Regional Breakdown of Possession Claims

item.title: Housing demand and sales are stagnant, says RICS
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market remains in a holding pattern, with buyer demand and completed sales showing little movement in July, according to the latest RICS Residential Market Survey. The report suggests ongoing economic uncertainties and mortgage affordability challenges continue to dampen market activity across most regions.

Market activity remains subdued

New buyer enquiries recorded a net balance of -28% in July, unchanged from June's figure. While this represents an improvement from March's low of -41%, it indicates demand remains significantly weaker than historical averages. Similarly, agreed sales held steady at -30%, mirroring June's results but showing some recovery from April's -37% reading.

Regional variations paint an uneven picture, with London, the South East and South West experiencing more pronounced price declines than the national average. Northern Ireland continues to buck the trend with rising prices, while Scotland's previously strong growth appears to be stabilising.

Price expectations reflect caution

Short-term price projections remain pessimistic, with a three-month outlook of -31%. The twelve-month forecast sits slightly more positive at +4%, though London stands out with particularly weak expectations at -23% - a notable drop from -10% in the previous survey.

Simon Rubinsohn, RICS Chief Economist, noted: "The combination of geopolitical tensions, domestic political uncertainty and mortgage affordability challenges continues to weigh on market sentiment. The subdued forward-looking indicators suggest this cautious climate may persist."

Louise Apollonio of Shawbrook added: "The typical summer uplift in activity hasn't materialised this year. Various factors including extreme weather, political changes and broader economic concerns appear to be causing many potential buyers to adopt a wait-and-see approach."

Looking ahead

Market observers suggest the upcoming Autumn Budget on 28th October could influence buyer behaviour, with some households potentially delaying decisions until the government's fiscal plans become clearer. The persistent cost-of-living pressures and mortgage rate volatility mean any significant market recovery may need to wait until 2024.

For those considering entering the market, comparing mortgage deals and seeking independent financial advice could help navigate the current climate. However, with price expectations varying significantly by region, local market research remains essential.

item.title: Another day, another PM, another Budget
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property market has long been a cornerstone of the nation’s economy, yet its potential is often hindered by political uncertainty and shifting fiscal policies. Historically, Budget announcements were made in March or April, allowing homeowners to prepare for the prime selling season. However, since 2017, the main Budget has been moved to late autumn, coinciding with a period of heightened political volatility. This shift has created apprehension among buyers, sellers, and investors, dampening what is traditionally the second-best period for property transactions.

The Impact of Political Instability

Over the past decade, the UK has experienced significant political upheaval, with frequent changes in leadership and policy direction. This instability has made it challenging for the property market to thrive, as uncertainty often leads to hesitation among buyers and sellers. The five-year political cycle, intended to provide stability, has been disrupted by early elections and shifting ideologies. As a result, long-term economic planning has become increasingly difficult, leaving the property sector without a cohesive strategy.

Unlike countries such as China, where a one-party system allows for consistent long-term planning, the UK’s political landscape is marked by frequent changes in leadership and policy. This unpredictability has discouraged private investment in property, as investors are wary of sudden shifts in taxation or regulation. With UK Property PLC accounting for around 10% of the nation’s economy, the lack of a coherent plan for the sector could have far-reaching consequences.

Proposing a Solution

To mitigate the impact of political uncertainty, some experts have suggested creating a council of property professionals to guide policy decisions. This council could include individuals with extensive experience in the property market, planning processes, and commercial imperatives. By leveraging their expertise, it may be possible to develop policies that support long-term investment and address the diverse needs of different regions and demographics.

Local mayoral input could also play a role in shaping property policy, ensuring that decisions reflect the unique challenges and opportunities of each area. However, detailed proposals for such a scheme are still lacking. Despite this, there is no shortage of experienced property professionals who are eager to contribute to solutions that benefit both homeowners and investors.

As the next Budget approaches on 28th October, there is hope that policymakers will prioritise sensible, long-term strategies over short-term political gains. History has shown that excessive taxation does not lead to sustainable growth, and a balanced approach will be essential to unlocking the full potential of the UK property market.

In a time of uncertainty, collaboration between policymakers and property experts could pave the way for a more stable and prosperous future. By focusing on coherent planning and fostering private investment, the UK property market can continue to thrive, benefiting homeowners, investors, and the wider economy alike.

item.title: Reaction to UK Finance mortgage arrears data
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent data from UK Finance reveals positive trends in mortgage arrears and possessions across both residential and buy-to-let sectors during the second quarter of 2026. The figures highlight lenders' ongoing commitment to supporting borrowers facing financial challenges, with notable quarterly improvements particularly evident in the rental property market.

Arrears show downward trend

The latest statistics indicate that 77,940 homeowner mortgages were in arrears of 2.5% or more of their outstanding balance during Q2 2026 – a modest 1% reduction compared to the previous quarter. The decline was more pronounced in the buy-to-let sector, where 8,390 BTL mortgages fell into this arrears category, marking a 6% quarterly improvement.

Industry experts suggest these reductions reflect both the effectiveness of lender support schemes and the gradual easing of broader economic pressures. However, commentators caution that affordability challenges persist for many households, emphasising the importance of early engagement with lenders when financial difficulties arise.

Possessions remain below historic averages

Repossession figures continue to show encouraging signs, remaining substantially lower than long-term historical averages. During Q2 2026, 1,150 residential properties were taken into possession – an 8% quarterly decrease and 14% annual reduction. The buy-to-let market saw more significant progress, with just 630 rental properties repossessed, representing a 22% quarterly decline and 20% annual improvement.

James Tatch, head of analytics at UK Finance, noted that this marks the first year-on-year decrease in possessions since late 2023. He reiterated that lenders maintain comprehensive support options for borrowers concerned about meeting repayments, with tailored assistance available through early dialogue.

Market stakeholders emphasise proactive approach

Property professionals have welcomed the positive trends while highlighting ongoing challenges in the housing market. NAEA Propertymark President Ian Harris pointed out that most current possessions relate to older mortgages, underlining the importance of continued collaboration between lenders, agents and policymakers to support at-risk borrowers.

Harris particularly emphasised the need for landlords to seek early advice when facing financial pressure, as rental property difficulties can have wider implications for housing availability. The property industry continues to advocate for preventative measures and early intervention strategies to help maintain market stability.

For homeowners or landlords experiencing repayment concerns, financial institutions recommend making contact at the earliest opportunity. Most lenders offer various support options, including temporary payment reductions, term extensions or switching to interest-only arrangements, with solutions tailored to individual circumstances.

item.title: Landlords ‘raising asking rents as bidding war ban hits’
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Following the introduction of Labour’s Renters’ Rights Act, landlords across the UK have been increasing their asking rents, according to recent reports. While this may seem counterintuitive, the trend appears to be linked to the Act’s ban on competitive bidding for rental properties. Letting agents and landlords are no longer permitted to encourage tenants to bid against one another, prompting many to set higher initial asking prices in anticipation of negotiations.

Impact of the Renters’ Rights Act

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced in May, initially brought a surge of activity to the rental market as landlords and tenants adjusted to the new rules. However, Chestertons, a leading estate agency, noted that this activity stabilised by July. The legislation’s prohibition on bidding wars has led landlords to adopt a different strategy. By setting higher asking rents, landlords aim to secure offers closer to their desired price, even if tenants negotiate downwards.

This shift in pricing strategies is beginning to reflect in rental market data. Rightmove’s Rental Trends Tracker highlights that asking rents rose by 2.9% year-on-year during the second quarter of 2026, marking the strongest growth rate in two years. London, in particular, saw rental growth outpace the rest of the UK for the first time since late 2023, with a 2.3% increase.

Market Dynamics and Tenant Demand

The trend of higher asking rents first emerged in June and has continued into July, albeit at a slower pace. Landlords appear to be growing more confident in their pricing strategies, particularly as supply levels in the rental market remain constrained. Many landlords are either selling properties or reducing their portfolios, while tenant demand continues to rise.

Katinka Hill, head of lettings at Chestertons, commented on the evolving market dynamics: “Activity seen immediately after the legislation was introduced in May eased off in July. However, in the first 10 days of August, our branches have seen applicant registrations up 18% year-on-year, which aligns with the seasonal summer uptick we would expect at this time of year.”

This combination of reduced supply and increased demand is likely to sustain upward pressure on rental prices in the coming months. Prospective tenants may wish to act swiftly to secure rental properties, particularly in high-demand areas like London.

As the rental market continues to adapt to the Renters’ Rights Act, both landlords and tenants will need to navigate these changes carefully. Landlords might consider setting realistic asking prices, whilst tenants could benefit from being well-prepared for negotiations in a competitive market.
